The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The **monic probabilists' Hermite polynomials** are the polynomials $H_m\in\mathbb R[x]$ defined by
$$H_0=1,\qquad H_1(x)=x,\qquad xH_m(x)=H_{m+1}(x)+m\,H_{m-1}(x)\quad(m\ge1).$$
The recurrence is solved for the higher polynomial, $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, so it determines $H_m$ uniquely by induction on $m$. Each $H_m$ is monic of degree $m$: $H_2=x^2-1$, $H_3=x^3-3x$ and $H_4=x^4-6x^2+3$; in general $H_m(x)=m!\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\frac{(-1/2)^j x^{m-2j}}{j!\,(m-2j)!}$.

Under the AC assumption of the Gaussian-law supplier, these are the monic orthogonal polynomials for the standard normal law of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: they form an orthogonal system for the measure $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}dx$; orthogonality and the expansion of monomials in this system are proved separately on this page. The moments of that law are those of [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], and the polynomial calculus used below is that of [[def-derivative]]. The defining property used in this batch is the recurrence; no choice principle is used.

Assume countable choice. On every measure space, complex $L^p$ is complete for $1\le p\le\infty$, and every norm-convergent sequence has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to its limit. For finite $p$, finite simple functions with finite-measure support are dense, and on $\mathbb R^n$ with Lebesgue measure, $n\ge1$, complex $C_c^\infty$ is dense. Complex $L^2$ has the first-variable-linear inner product $\int f\overline g$, its norm is $\|\cdot\|_2$, and Cauchy–Schwarz has the following equality criterion: if $g\ne0$, equality iff $f=cg$ a.e.; if $g=0$, equality for all $f$. The finite-tuple version uses a common scalar across components.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

For every $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n\ge1$, the integral defining $\widehat f(\xi)$ is absolutely convergent for every $\xi$ and unchanged by null-set modifications. Moreover $|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\|f\|_1$.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

Put $v(x)=r(x)\phi(x)$, so $v\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ by [F1] and [F6]. For every $a\ge0$, Cauchy–Schwarz and completion of the square give $\int |r(x)|e^{a|x|}\,d\gamma(x)\le\|r\|_2(\int e^{2a|x|}\,d\gamma)^{1/2}<\infty$, since each half-line integral is at most $e^{2a^2}$.

Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R$. The partial sums $S_M(x)=\sum_{j=0}^M(-2\pi i\xi x)^j/j!$ converge pointwise to $e^{-2\pi i\xi x}$ and satisfy $|S_M(x)|\le e^{2\pi|\xi||x|}$ by [F5]. Applying [F7] with the integrable majorant from step 1.2 gives $\widehat v(\xi)=\lim_{M\to\infty}\int r(x)S_M(x)\,d\gamma(x)=0$, because every term is a scalar multiple of a zero moment from step 1.1.

By [F4], $\widehat v=0$ implies $v=0$ Lebesgue-almost everywhere. Since $\phi(x)>0$ for all $x$, $r=0$ $\gamma$-almost everywhere. Thus the only $L^2(\gamma)$ function orthogonal to all the $h_m$ is zero.

For arbitrary real $f\in L^2(\gamma)$, set $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $S_M=\sum_{m=0}^M a_mh_m$. Orthogonality in [F2] gives $\|f-S_M\|_2^2=\|f\|_2^2-\sum_{m=0}^M a_m^2\ge0$ and, for $M>K$, $\|S_M-S_K\|_2^2=\sum_{K<m\le M}a_m^2$; hence the partial sums are Cauchy. View them in complex $L^2(\gamma)$; by [F3] and [A1] they converge there, and their limit is real because every $S_M$ is real. The residual $f-S$ is orthogonal to each $h_m$, hence zero by step 3.1. If only finitely many $a_m$ are nonzero, step 4.1 makes $f$ equal almost everywhere to a polynomial $p$. If $f$ is continuous and differs from $p$ at some point, it differs on a nonempty open interval, which has positive $\gamma$ measure by [F1]; hence $f=p$ everywhere, contrary to nonpolynomiality. Thus a continuous nonpolynomial $f$ has unbounded coefficient support. A globally Lipschitz $f$ obeys $|f(x)|\le |f(0)|+L|x|$; [F8] gives $\int |x|^2\,d\gamma<\infty$, so this growth bound implies $f\in L^2(\gamma)$.

The continuous difference quotients $s_n(x)=n(\sigma(x+1/n)-\sigma(x))$ are bounded in modulus by the Lipschitz constant; their pointwise upper limit is a bounded Borel function and equals $\sigma'(x)$ wherever the derivative exists. The product standard-normal density is positive on every nonempty open box; since $A^{-1}$ maps nonempty open sets to nonempty open sets, $Z=AG$ assigns positive probability to every nonempty open set in $\mathbb R^m$.
By [F2], each $Z_i$ has a scalar normal law with variance $C_{ii}>0$, hence a density. Therefore changing $s$ on the exceptional null set changes none of the random variables $s(Z_i)$ almost surely.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, let $H_m$ be the monic probabilists’ Hermite polynomial defined by $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=x$, and $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, and put $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$. Then $(h_m)_{m\ge0}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of real $L^2(\gamma)$. Every $f\in L^2(\gamma)$ has the norm-convergent expansion $f=\sum_{m\ge0}a_mh_m$, where $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$. If $f$ is continuous and nonpolynomial, then $a_m\ne0$ for an unbounded set of indices $m$. Every globally Lipschitz real function belongs to $L^2(\gamma)$, so this conclusion applies to every globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation.

The **monic probabilists' Hermite polynomials** are the polynomials $H_m\in\mathbb R[x]$ defined by
$$H_0=1,\qquad H_1(x)=x,\qquad xH_m(x)=H_{m+1}(x)+m\,H_{m-1}(x)\quad(m\ge1).$$
The recurrence is solved for the higher polynomial, $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, so it determines $H_m$ uniquely by induction on $m$. Each $H_m$ is monic of degree $m$: $H_2=x^2-1$, $H_3=x^3-3x$ and $H_4=x^4-6x^2+3$; in general $H_m(x)=m!\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\frac{(-1/2)^j x^{m-2j}}{j!\,(m-2j)!}$.

Under the AC assumption of the Gaussian-law supplier, these are the monic orthogonal polynomials for the standard normal law of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: they form an orthogonal system for the measure $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}dx$; orthogonality and the expansion of monomials in this system are proved separately on this page. The moments of that law are those of [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], and the polynomial calculus used below is that of [[def-derivative]]. The defining property used in this batch is the recurrence; no choice principle is used.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. The canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Since $\nabla C$ is locally Lipschitz, the vector field $-A\nabla C$ is locally Lipschitz and [F3] gives a unique local solution.

abla C$ give $\langle
abla C(z),z_*-zangle\le C(z_*)-C(z)$. Along any solution, expanding the squared inverse-metric norm to first order then gives $ rac{d}{dt}\|z-z_*\|_{A^{-1}}^2=-2\langle z-z_*,
abla C(z)angle\le-2(C(z)-C(z_*))\le0.$ Hence the solution remains in the closed $A^{-1}$-metric ball centered at $z_*$ through $z_0$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $h_0:\Theta\to H$, $\Phi_t:\Theta\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$, and $\ell:\Theta\times H\to\mathbb R$ are continuously differentiable on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta$. A continuously differentiable map is totally differentiable at each point and has a derivative matrix continuous on its domain. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. Write $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, with each partial derivative holding the other argument fixed. Set $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$ and, in descending order, $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$. Then the backpropagation algorithm returns $J(\theta)$ and

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0,$$

where the sum is empty when $T=0$. The statement also applies when every primitive is evaluated on one fixed strict $C^1$ branch; it makes no assertion at a branch boundary.

Let $P,q\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^P$ be open, let $X$ be a set, and let $f:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R^q$. Fix $\theta\in\Omega$ and suppose that for each $x\in X$ the map $\vartheta\mapsto f(\vartheta,x)$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$, meaning it has a linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|\vartheta-\theta\|_2)$. Write $D_\theta f(\theta,x)\in\mathbb R^{q\times P}$ for its derivative matrix in the standard Euclidean coordinates. The matrix-valued neural tangent kernel at $\theta$ is

$$K_\theta(x,x'):=D_\theta f(\theta,x)\,D_\theta f(\theta,x')^{T}\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}.$$

Equivalently, for $1\le a,b\le q$,
$$\bigl(K_\theta(x,x')\bigr)_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f_a(\theta,x)\,\partial_{\theta_p}f_b(\theta,x').$$
For a scalar-output model this is the scalar kernel $\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x)\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x')$.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, differentiable except at countably
many points, and $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, then $F$ is absolutely continuous and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt$$
for every $x\in[a,b]$.

Here division by $N$ acts on the data sum.

For an array $R\in\mathbb R^{m\times N}$ write $\|R\|_{F,N}=\|R\|_F/\sqrt N$. Let $c=\sup|\sigma'|$ and $M_2=\sup|\sigma''|$, both finite by the hypotheses (taking a difference-quotient limit in the global Lipschitz inequality gives $c\le\operatorname{Lip}(\sigma)$), and set $w_\ell(t)=\|W^{(\ell)}(t)\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ and $a_\ell(t)=\|Z^\ell(t)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ for $1\le\ell<L$. The initial block and layerwise chain rule give $B_1\le\|X\|_F^2/(n_0N)+\beta^2$ and $B_{\ell+1}\le c^2w_\ell^2B_\ell+a_\ell^2+\beta^2$ for $1\le\ell<L$: the current-layer weight-and-bias Gram has operator norm at most $a_\ell^2+\beta^2$, while the preceding Jacobian is composed with $W^{(\ell)}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ and diagonal activation derivatives of norm at most $c$. The backpropagation identity in step 1.1 also gives $\|D^\ell(t)\|_{F,N}\le c^{L-\ell}(\prod_{k=\ell}^{L-1}w_k(t))\|d(t)\|_N$. Recursively, each $B_\ell$ is bounded by a polynomial in the finitely many $a_k,w_k,c,\beta$, and each backpropagation norm is bounded by such a polynomial times $\|d(t)\|_N$.

For hidden layers the chain rule gives $\dot U^\ell=-\mathcal K^\ell D^\ell$, so $\|\dot U^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le B_\ell\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$; for $\ell=1$ this is the first-layer parameter Gram. The hidden-bias equation gives $\beta\|\dot b^{(\ell-1)}\|_2/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le\beta^2\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, and the first-layer matrix gives $\|\dot W^{(0)}\|_F/\sqrt{n_1}\le C\|D^1\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_1}$ with $C=\|X\|_F/\sqrt{n_0N}$. The output bias is excluded because its derivative contributes only the constant feature $\beta$ and changes no later feature or parameter derivative. By [F7], $|\sigma'(u)-\sigma\prime(v)|\le M_2|u-v|$; global Lipschitz continuity gives $\|\dot Z^\ell\|_{F,N}\le c\|\dot U^\ell\|_{F,N}$. For $1\le\ell<L$ define $\widetilde a_\ell=\|Z^\ell(t)-Z^\ell(0)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, $\widetilde u_\ell=\|U^\ell(t)-U^\ell(0)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, and $\widetilde w_\ell=\|W^{(\ell)}(t)-W^{(\ell)}(0)\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$; for $0\le\ell<L-1$ put $\widetilde b_\ell=\beta\|b^{(\ell)}(t)-b^{(\ell)}(0)\|_2/\sqrt{n_{\ell+1}}$, and put $\widetilde w_0=\|W^{(0)}(t)-W^{(0)}(0)\|_F/\sqrt{n_1}$. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

Assume AC. Let $C_n$ be real symmetric positive-semidefinite $2\times2$ matrices converging entrywise to $C$, and suppose both diagonal entries of $C_n$ and of $C$ are positive. Let $(U_n,V_n)$ and $(U,V)$ have centered bivariate normal laws with covariance matrices $C_n$ and $C$, respectively; singular covariance matrices are allowed. For every globally Lipschitz $\tau:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[\tau(U_n)\tau(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[\tau(U)\tau(V)].$$
For every bounded Borel function $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[g(U_n)g(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[g(U)g(V)].$$
The second conclusion applies to any bounded measurable representative of an almost-everywhere derivative, including when the limiting pair is supported on a line.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume AC. Fix a finite data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a horizon $T\ge0$. Let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz, twice continuously differentiable, and have bounded second derivative. Use the network parameterization and independent standard-normal initialization in the width-normalized network definition, with scalar output $n_L=1$. For each hidden-width tuple $(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, suppose a differentiable parameter path exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)\,d_i(t),$$

where $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable. Write $K_t=(K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$ for the finite-data scalar neural tangent kernel. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_N\,dt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential hidden-width limit, where $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$ and stochastic boundedness means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ satisfies the iterated-limit upper bound $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)<\varepsilon$. Then, as $n_1\to\infty$ first and then $n_2,\ldots,n_{L-1}\to\infty$, for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}>\varepsilon\right)\longrightarrow0.$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

derivations.claim: By [F8], $\sigma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact interval; applying [F9] on $[-m,m]$ for each positive integer $m$ shows that it is differentiable outside a Lebesgue-null set. The forward difference quotients $s_0(x)=\limsup_{k\to\infty}k(\sigma(x+1/k)-\sigma(x))$ define a bounded Borel function and equal $\sigma\prime(x)$ wherever the derivative exists. Since the given representative $s$ also equals $\sigma\prime$ almost everywhere, there is a Lebesgue-null set $E$ outside which $\sigma$ is differentiable and $s=s_0=\sigma\prime$. For any fixed finite width tuple, condition on the preceding layers: every coordinate of every data-point preactivation is normal with variance $\|z^\ell(x_i)\|_2^2/n_\ell+\beta^2\ge\beta^2$. Thus each avoids $E$ almost surely, and a finite union shows all preactivations at initialization avoid $E$ almost surely. The finite network is therefore parameter-differentiable at initialization for every data point, and [F5] applies with derivative values $s(U)$. The first-layer covariance is $\Sigma^1$; its diagonal is positive, and its Jacobian Gram block is exactly $K^1_{(i,a),(j,b)}=\delta_{ab}\Sigma^1_{ij}$ because different neurons use disjoint parameters.

Let $C_n$ be the conditional empirical covariance of the layer-$(r-1)$ preactivation vectors across the $n_{r-1}$ neurons. By induction $C_n\to\Sigma^{r-1}$ in probability; conditional on the preceding layer, these vectors are iid centered Gaussian with covariance $C_n$ and diagonal entries at least $\beta^2$. Choose $R>1+\max_i\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii}$, so $\mathbb P(\max_i(C_n)_{ii}>R)\to0$. Write $L_\sigma$ for a global Lipschitz constant. If $Y_a=\sigma(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))\sigma(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$, the Lipschitz bound $|\sigma(u)|\le|\sigma(0)|+L_\sigma|u|$, Gaussian fourth moments, and Cauchy--Schwarz give $\mathbb E[Y_a^2\mid C_n]\le M_R$ whenever all diagonal entries of $C_n$ are at most $R$, for a finite constant $M_R$. The conditional variance bound in [F3] therefore gives $\mathbb P(|n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_aY_a-\mathbb E[Y_a\mid C_n]|>\eta)\le\mathbb P(\max_i(C_n)_{ii}>R)+M_R/(n_{r-1}\eta^2)\to0$. The conditional mean is a bivariate Gaussian feature expectation and converges by [F4] to $\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]$. For $V_a=s(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))s(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$, the same conditional variance estimate holds with $M_R=\|s\|_\infty^4$, and [F4] makes its conditional mean converge to $\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$. Adding the bias Gram gives $\Sigma^r$. Each empirical feature Gram plus that bias Gram is positive semidefinite with diagonal at least $\beta^2$; the cone of positive-semidefinite matrices is closed, so its deterministic limit $\Sigma^r$ is positive semidefinite and defines the next Gaussian pairs. This proves the covariance and derivative recursions at every layer.

For a finite network, [F5] gives the exact tangent-kernel block recursion $K^{r}_{(i,c),(j,d)}=\delta_{cd}(n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_a Z^{r-1}_{ai}Z^{r-1}_{aj}+\beta^2)+n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_{a,b}W^{(r-1)}_{ca}W^{(r-1)}_{db}s(U^{r-1}_{ai})s(U^{r-1}_{bj})K^{r-1}_{(i,a),(j,b)}$. The first term is the current-layer weight-and-bias Gram, and the second is the contribution of all earlier shared parameters. At the first layer this block is the one in step 1.1.

At this sequential stage the previous widths have already been taken to their limits while $n_{r-1}$ and $n_r$ are fixed, so the inductive block has limit $K^{r-1}_{(i,a),(j,b)}=\delta_{ab}\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}$ for the finitely many $a,b$. Substituting this block in the Jacobian term of step 2.2 leaves $\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_a W^{(r-1)}_{ca}W^{(r-1)}_{da}q_a$, where $q_a=s(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))s(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$ and $|q_a|\le\|s\|_\infty^2$. The current weights are independent standard normals, independent of the preceding $U$ values. Conditional on those values, for $c=d$ the mean is $\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_aq_a$ and the variance is at most $2(\Theta^{r-1}_{ij})^2\|s\|_\infty^4/n_{r-1}$, using $\operatorname{Var}(W^2)=2$; for $c\ne d$ the mean is zero and the variance is at most $(\Theta^{r-1}_{ij})^2\|s\|_\infty^4/n_{r-1}$, using independence of the two rows. The empirical average of $q_a$ converges to $\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$ by step 2.1, so the Jacobian term converges to $\delta_{cd}\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$. The covariance term converges to $\delta_{cd}\Sigma^r_{ij}$ by steps 2.1–2.2. Hence the limiting block is $\delta_{cd}(\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij})=\delta_{cd}\Theta^r_{ij}$. Since the final layer has one output, its scalar block is $K_\infty$.

Under the additional $C^2$ training hypotheses, [F6] and the initialization convergence from step 3.1 give $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\le\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{op}+\|K_0-K_\infty\|_{op}\to0$ in probability. The parameter-flow equation and [F5] give $\dot f_t(x_i)=-N^{-1}\sum_jK_t(i,j)d_j(t)$. Integrating and subtracting the equation with $K_\infty$ yields $\sup_{t\le T}\|f_t-f_0+N^{-1}\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\|_N\le N^{-1}\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\int_0^T\|d(s)\|_Nds$. For any $M>0$ and $\delta>0$, the product exceeds $\delta$ only if $\int_0^T\|d(s)\|_Nds>M$ or $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}>\delta N/M$; first use stochastic boundedness to choose $M$, then use kernel convergence. Thus the right side tends to zero in probability.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, let $H_m$ be the monic probabilists’ Hermite polynomial defined by $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=x$, and $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, and put $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$. Then $(h_m)_{m\ge0}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of real $L^2(\gamma)$. Every $f\in L^2(\gamma)$ has the norm-convergent expansion $f=\sum_{m\ge0}a_mh_m$, where $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$. If $f$ is continuous and nonpolynomial, then $a_m\ne0$ for an unbounded set of indices $m$. Every globally Lipschitz real function belongs to $L^2(\gamma)$, so this conclusion applies to every globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be standard Gaussian measure, let $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ be the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis, and let $f,g\in L^2(\gamma)$ have coefficients $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $b_m=\int g h_m\,d\gamma$. For $\rho\in[-1,1]$, let $(X,Y)$ have the centered bivariate normal law with unit variances and correlation $\rho$. Then
$$\mathbb E[f(X)g(Y)]=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}a_mb_m\rho^m.$$
The series is absolutely convergent, including at $\rho=\pm1$. In particular, the Gaussian dual kernel of $f$ is $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2\rho^m$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$.

Assume AC. Fix an integer $n_0\ge1$, a number $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. Let $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, put $q=n_0^{-1}+\beta^2$, and define $\mu(z)=\sigma(\sqrt q\,z)$. Let $a_m=\int \mu(z)h_m(z)\,d\gamma(z)$ be its coefficients in the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ of standard Gaussian measure $\gamma$. For $x,y\in S^{n_0-1}$, let $(U_{x,y},V_{x,y})$ be a centered Gaussian pair with variances $q$ and covariance $\beta^2+x\cdot y/n_0$, and set $k(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{x,y})\sigma(V_{x,y})]+\beta^2$. Then $k$ is strictly positive definite on $S^{n_0-1}$: for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$, $\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)>0$. The conclusion includes $n_0=1$, for which the sphere consists of the two points $-1$ and $1$.

Assume AC. Let $m\ge1$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ have the centered multivariate normal law with covariance $C$, let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz and nonconstant, and let $\beta>0$. Let $s$ be a bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$: it agrees with the ordinary derivative wherever that derivative exists, and its values on the remaining Lebesgue-null set are arbitrary. Define
$$S_{ij}:=\mathbb E[\sigma(Z_i)\sigma(Z_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad D_{ij}:=\mathbb E[s(Z_i)s(Z_j)]\quad(1\le i,j\le m).$$
Then $S$ is strictly positive definite and $D$ is positive semidefinite. Consequently, for every positive-semidefinite matrix $T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, the matrix $T\circ D+S$ is strictly positive definite, where $\circ$ denotes entrywise multiplication.

Let $P,q\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^P$ be open, let $X$ be a set, and let $f:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R^q$. Fix $\theta\in\Omega$ and suppose that for each $x\in X$ the map $\vartheta\mapsto f(\vartheta,x)$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$, meaning it has a linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|\vartheta-\theta\|_2)$. Write $D_\theta f(\theta,x)\in\mathbb R^{q\times P}$ for its derivative matrix in the standard Euclidean coordinates. The matrix-valued neural tangent kernel at $\theta$ is

$$K_\theta(x,x'):=D_\theta f(\theta,x)\,D_\theta f(\theta,x')^{T}\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}.$$

Equivalently, for $1\le a,b\le q$,
$$\bigl(K_\theta(x,x')\bigr)_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f_a(\theta,x)\,\partial_{\theta_p}f_b(\theta,x').$$
For a scalar-output model this is the scalar kernel $\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x)\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x')$.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

Assume AC. Fix a finite list $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Let $s$ be any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$, meaning that it agrees with the ordinary derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set; such a representative exists and is bounded by the Lipschitz constant. For every tuple of positive integer hidden widths $(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, use the width-normalized network with independent standard-normal initialization and scalar linear output.

Put

$$\Sigma^1_{ij}=\frac{x_i\cdot x_j}{n_0}+\beta^2.$$

For $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U_i,U_j)$ have the centered Gaussian law with variances $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii},\Sigma^{r-1}_{jj}$ and covariance $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ij}$, and define

$$\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad \dot\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[s(U_i)s(U_j)].$$

These Gaussian laws may be singular; their marginal variances are at least $\beta^2$, and their laws and expectations depend only on the displayed covariance. Define $\Theta^1_{ij}=\Sigma^1_{ij}$ and, for $r=2,\ldots,L$,

$$\Theta^r_{ij}=\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Sigma^r_{ij},\qquad K_\infty=(\Theta^L_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N.$$

At initialization, the finite-data neural tangent Gram matrix $K_0$ converges in probability to $K_\infty$ under the sequential hidden-width limit $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}$.

For the training conclusion, fix a horizon $T\ge0$. In addition, assume that $\sigma$ is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second derivative, that $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable, and that for each width tuple a differentiable parameter path $\theta(t)$ exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)d_i(t).$$

Write $f_t(x)=f_{\theta(t)}(x)$ and $K_t(i,j)=K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j)$, where $K_\theta$ is the finite-network neural tangent kernel. Define $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential limit, meaning that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ makes the iterated-limit upper bound on $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)$ less than $\varepsilon$. For the training conclusion, fix a horizon $T\ge0$. In addition, assume that $\sigma$ is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second derivative, that $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable, and that for each width tuple a differentiable parameter path $\theta(t)$ exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)d_i(t).$$

Write $f_t(x)=f_{\theta(t)}(x)$ and $K_t(i,j)=K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j)$, where $K_\theta$ is the finite-network neural tangent kernel. Define $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential limit, meaning that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ makes the iterated-limit upper bound on $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)$ less than $\varepsilon$. Then

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$

where $\|\cdot\|_{op}$ is the Euclidean operator norm. Along the path,

$$\dot f_t(x_i)=-\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K_t(i,j)d_j(t),$$

and

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\|f_t-f_0+\frac1N\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\right\|_N\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability}.$$

Thus the finite-time output equation has the deterministic limiting kernel as its generator in the precise integrated-error sense displayed above.

Let $P,q\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^P$ be open, let $X$ be a set, and let $f:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R^q$. Fix $\theta\in\Omega$ and suppose that for each $x\in X$ the map $\vartheta\mapsto f(\vartheta,x)$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$, meaning it has a linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|\vartheta-\theta\|_2)$. Write $D_\theta f(\theta,x)\in\mathbb R^{q\times P}$ for its derivative matrix in the standard Euclidean coordinates. The matrix-valued neural tangent kernel at $\theta$ is

$$K_\theta(x,x'):=D_\theta f(\theta,x)\,D_\theta f(\theta,x')^{T}\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}.$$

Equivalently, for $1\le a,b\le q$,
$$\bigl(K_\theta(x,x')\bigr)_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f_a(\theta,x)\,\partial_{\theta_p}f_b(\theta,x').$$
For a scalar-output model this is the scalar kernel $\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x)\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x')$.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

derivations.claim: Put $a=e^{2u}>0$. Then $|a-1|<a+1$, so $|\sigma(u)|<1$. The derivative rules in [F1] give $\sigma'(u)=4e^{2u}/(e^{2u}+1)^2=1-\sigma(u)^2$ and $\sigma''(u)=-2\sigma(u)\sigma'(u)$. Thus $|\sigma'|\le1$ and $|\sigma''|\le2$. By [F2], $|\sigma(u)-\sigma(v)|\le|u-v|$, so $\sigma$ is globally Lipschitz. Since $\sigma'(u)>0$, it is nonconstant; a polynomial of degree $m\ge1$ with leading coefficient $a_m\ne0$ satisfies $p(u)/u^m\to a_m$ as $u\to+\infty$, so its absolute value is unbounded. The bounded nonconstant $\sigma$ is therefore nonpolynomial.

For each finite network, the parameter vector field for the constant direction is smooth and locally Lipschitz, so a local solution exists by [F3]. The output-layer weights and bias have bounded speed because all hidden activations are bounded by $1$, so they remain bounded on every compact time interval. Suppose the parameters in layers $k+1,\ldots,L-1$ are bounded on such an interval. Backpropagating through those layers multiplies the direction by their finite weight matrices and factors $\sigma'$ of modulus at most $1$, so each coordinate of the backpropagated direction at layer $k+1$ is bounded. The gradient formulas in [F4], together with $|\sigma|\le1$, then bound every derivative in layer $k$; integration bounds its weights and biases. Descending induction bounds all parameters on every compact interval. If the maximal local solution had a finite endpoint, the smooth vector field would be bounded on a compact ball containing the trajectory, so the trajectory would be Lipschitz in time and have a limit as the endpoint is approached. Applying [F3] at that limit extends the solution, a contradiction. Hence the path exists on $[0,1]$. On any compact tube around a finite solution segment the vector field is Lipschitz; subtracting the integral equations for two solutions gives $u(t)\le u(0)+M\int_0^tu(s)\,ds$ on the tube for a Lipschitz constant $M$; iterating this inequality gives $u(t)\le e^{Mt}u(0)$, proving local continuous dependence on the initial parameters. A finite cover of $[0,1]$ patches these local flow maps. Thus the global path is measurable as a function of initialization and time. For this direction, $\|d(t)\|_N=1$ at every time, so its integral is $1$.

Step 1.1 supplies the globally Lipschitz $C^2$ activation and bounded second derivative, and step 2.1 supplies a finite-width solution and the required direction bound. Applying [F4] with $T=1$ gives $\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\to0$ in probability under the stated sequential hidden-width limit.

Assume AC. Fix $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. For $x,y$ on the unit sphere $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, define $\Sigma^1(x,y)=x\cdot y/n_0+\beta^2$. Recursively, for $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U,V)$ be a centered Gaussian pair whose covariance entries are $\Sigma^{r-1}(x,x),\Sigma^{r-1}(y,y),\Sigma^{r-1}(x,y)$, and set

$$\Sigma^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U)\sigma(V)]+\beta^2,\qquad D^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[s(U)s(V)],$$

where $s$ is any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$. Set $\Theta^1=\Sigma^1$ and $\Theta^r(x,y)=\Theta^{r-1}(x,y)D^r(x,y)+\Sigma^r(x,y)$. Then for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^{n_0-1}$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$,

$$\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_ic_j\Theta^L(x_i,x_j)>0.$$

Thus the scalar limiting neural tangent kernel is strictly positive definite on every finite set of distinct sphere points, for every $n_0\ge1$ and $L\ge2$. In dimension $n_0=1$ this includes both antipodal points of $S^0=\{-1,1\}$.

Assume AC and use the source-normalized network with scalar output, a finite data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ with $N\ge1$, and limiting neural tangent Gram matrix $K_\infty$ from the sequential infinite-width theorem. For a target vector $y\in\mathbb R^N$, consider the finite-data least-squares loss $\mathcal L(f)=\frac1{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N(f_i-y_i)^2$ and its limiting kernel-gradient-flow equation

$$\dot f(t)=-\frac1N K_\infty(f(t)-y),\qquad f(0)=f_0.$$

Let $K_\infty=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)Q^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $\lambda_i\ge0$. Then for every $t\ge0$,

$$\bigl(Q^T(f(t)-y)\bigr)_i=e^{-t\lambda_i/N}\,\bigl(Q^T(f_0-y)\bigr)_i\quad(1\le i\le N).$$

Zero-eigenvalue residual components remain constant. If the inputs are pairwise distinct points on $S^{n_0-1}$, with $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation, then $K_\infty$ is positive definite and $f(t)\to y$ as $t\to\infty$.
